stem: A Tier 1 analyst receives a SIEM alert: 14 failed logins followed by a successful login to a finance server. Following a standard SOC workflow, what should the analyst do NEXT?

options.text: Reimage the finance server now to remove any attacker foothold before it spreads
options.why: Order: containment before triage. You don't yet know this is a real incident, and reimaging destroys the evidence you'd need.

options.text: Triage the alert: check source, account, timing and context to confirm if it's real
options.why: Correct. Triage (real or noise?) comes right after an alert fires and decides whether to investigate further or close.

options.text: Reset the account's password and notify the user their login may be compromised
options.why: Order: a reasonable containment step, but taken before triage confirms anything. It also loses context, such as whether the source is a known device.

options.text: Escalate to Tier 2 with the raw alert attached so a senior analyst can investigate
options.why: Order: escalation follows triage. Passing up an untriaged alert spends Tier 2 time on something that may be noise.

explanation: The SOC workflow runs: alert → triage → investigation → escalation if needed → containment/remediation → documentation. Triage comes first so analysts spend time on real threats.

stem: A SOC is redefining its tiers. Which TWO responsibilities belong at Tier 3 rather than Tier 1? (Choose two.)

options.text: Proactive threat hunting for activity that hasn't triggered any alerts
options.why: Correct. Hunting assumes compromise and searches beyond existing alerts, which is Tier 3 work.

options.text: Monitoring the alert queue and performing first-pass triage on new alerts
options.why: This is the core Tier 1 job.

options.text: Advanced analysis, such as reverse-engineering a malware sample
options.why: Correct. Deep technical analysis sits at Tier 3.

options.text: Owning the SOC's metrics, reporting and escalation policy
options.why: This is the SOC manager's role (oversight, metrics, escalation ownership), not an analyst tier.

explanation: Tier 1 triages, Tier 2 investigates in depth, Tier 3 hunts threats and does advanced analysis, and the SOC manager owns oversight and metrics.

stem: A SOC lead reviews this weekly rule report. Which action would BEST reduce analyst workload without losing the rule's detection value?
artifact:
SOC weekly rule report (week 40)
Rule: VPN-ImpossibleTravel-01
Alerts fired:            214
Closed false positive:   133 (62%)
  top FP reason: user egress via corporate VPN concentrator 198.51.100.10
True positive:           4
Median triage time:      41 min

options.text: Tune the rule to exclude the known VPN egress address, then track its precision
options.why: Correct. The false positives share one known, benign cause. Tuning that out keeps the rule's real detections and frees triage time.

options.text: Lower the rule's severity so its alerts queue quietly instead of paging
options.why: Scope: it hides the noise instead of removing its cause, and the 4 true positives now get slower attention.

options.text: Use a SOAR playbook to auto-close every alert this rule raises
options.why: Scope: automating closure removes the triage cost, but it also closes the 4 true positives. Automation should target the known benign cause, not the whole rule.

options.text: Batch-review this rule's alerts once a week instead of triaging them live
options.why: Timing: it gives up continuous monitoring, so a real impossible-travel login could sit unanswered for days.

explanation: Process improvement (1.5) targets the root cause of noise. One documented false-positive source makes a precise tuning candidate, and measuring precision afterwards confirms the change worked.

stem: A company moves its HR application from its own data centre to an IaaS provider. Under the shared responsibility model, which task does the company STILL own?

options.text: Physical security of the provider's data centre and its staff access
options.why: The provider owns physical facilities in every cloud model.

options.text: Patching the hypervisors that host the company's virtual machines
options.why: The IaaS provider manages the virtualisation layer.

options.text: Configuring IAM permissions and protecting data in its workloads
options.why: Correct. Identities, configurations, workloads and data stay with the customer.

options.text: Replacing failed disks in the provider's storage arrays
options.why: Hardware is the provider's responsibility.

explanation: Cloud shifts physical infrastructure to the provider, but the customer always keeps its data, identities (IAM) and the security of its workload configurations.

stem: In a software-defined network, a central controller calculates paths and pushes flow rules to the switches. Which SDN plane is the controller operating in?

options.text: Data plane
options.why: The data plane forwards packets according to the rules it has received. It doesn't decide them.

options.text: Control plane
options.why: Correct. The control plane decides how traffic should flow and programs the data plane.

options.text: Management plane
options.why: The management plane handles admin access, configuration and monitoring of the devices.

options.text: Application plane
options.why: Adjacent concept: true, some SDN models put applications above the controller, where they express intent through northbound APIs. But the controller itself operates in the control plane.

explanation: SDN separates the control plane (decisions, centralised in the controller) from the data plane (forwarding). The management plane covers administration. Centralised control means faster, consistent policy changes.

stem: An analyst correlates these events from a hybrid environment. What should the analyst do FIRST?
artifact:
[onprem-dc01] 2026-10-08T02:14:07Z EventID=4624 LogonType=10 User=CORP\j.tan Src=203.0.113.50
[cloudtrail]  2026-10-08T02:16:42Z eventName=ConsoleLogin user=j.tan sourceIPAddress=203.0.113.50 MFAUsed=No
[cloudtrail]  2026-10-08T02:18:03Z eventName=CreateAccessKey user=j.tan sourceIPAddress=203.0.113.50

options.text: Contain j.tan's identity: disable the new access key and the account, then investigate
options.why: Correct. The same external IP reached on-prem RDP and the cloud console without MFA, then created a persistent credential. The identity is the attack path, so contain it first.

options.text: Pull 30 days of CloudTrail history for j.tan to scope the activity before changing anything
options.why: Order: scoping is needed, but not before containment. The new access key gives the attacker persistent access while you search.

options.text: Block 203.0.113.50 at the on-prem perimeter firewall and monitor for new attempts
options.why: Scope: the cloud console is reached over the internet, not through your perimeter, and the new access key works from any IP.

options.text: Force a password reset for CORP\j.tan in Active Directory and end the RDP session
options.why: Scope: it shuts the on-prem path, but the cloud access key created at 02:18 stays valid even if the cloud identity is federated.

explanation: In cloud/hybrid environments IAM is the perimeter. One external IP using one identity on-prem and in the cloud, with no MFA and a new access key created (persistence), calls for containing the identity first.

stem: A storage bucket was exposed publicly by a Terraform template that went through code review unnoticed. Which control would BEST stop the same mistake reaching production again?

options.text: Scan IaC templates in the CI pipeline (e.g. Checkov) and fail builds on exposure
options.why: Correct. It catches the misconfiguration before deployment by treating infrastructure templates as code that needs security review.

options.text: Rely on GuardDuty findings to alert the team when a bucket becomes public
options.why: Timing: true, GuardDuty can flag risky S3 changes, but only after deployment. By then the bucket is already exposed.

options.text: Add a mandatory second reviewer to every Terraform pull request
options.why: Scope: human review already missed this once. A second reviewer helps, but it won't consistently catch misconfigurations the way an automated policy check does.

options.text: Enable AWS Config rules that flag public buckets and auto-remediate them after deploy
options.why: Timing: a strong backstop, but it acts after deployment. The template keeps producing the misconfiguration, and each deploy is briefly exposed.

explanation: IaC misconfigurations are a top cloud attack vector. Pre-deployment scanning (Checkov, Prisma Cloud) is the preventive control. Runtime detection is a backstop, not a replacement.

stem: An analyst is investigating suspicious activity in an AWS account. Which TWO log sources are generated natively by AWS and most relevant? (Choose two.)

options.text: AWS CloudTrail
options.why: Correct. It records API and console activity: who did what, from where.

options.text: VPC Flow Logs
options.why: Correct. They capture network flow metadata for traffic in the VPC.

options.text: Microsoft Sentinel
options.why: This is Azure's cloud SIEM. It can ingest AWS logs, but it isn't an AWS log source.

options.text: Azure Activity Log
options.why: This records Azure control-plane events, not AWS.

explanation: Know the platform-native sources. AWS: CloudTrail (API activity), VPC Flow Logs (network) and GuardDuty (threat detection). Azure: Sentinel (SIEM) and Defender for Cloud.

stem: After a cloud incident, the team wants to map the attacker's behaviour (abusing valid cloud accounts, discovering storage, exfiltrating to an external bucket) to a standard adversary framework. Which reference fits BEST?

options.text: MITRE ATT&CK Cloud Matrix
options.why: Correct. It catalogues adversary tactics and techniques specific to cloud platforms.

options.text: OWASP API Top 10
options.why: This lists API vulnerability classes, not adversary behaviour across an intrusion.

options.text: CVSS v4.0 base metrics
options.why: CVSS scores the severity of individual vulnerabilities. It doesn't map attacker behaviour.

options.text: NIST CSF 2.0 functions
options.why: NIST CSF is a program-level framework (Govern, Identify, Protect…). It doesn't catalogue adversary techniques.

explanation: The ATT&CK Cloud Matrix is the tactical reference for mapping cloud incidents to adversary tactics and techniques.

stem: A security lead says perimeter-focused monitoring won't protect a new app built from microservices, serverless functions and short-lived containers. Which characteristic BEST explains why?

options.text: Its attack surface is spread across many small, short-lived components and APIs
options.why: Correct. Many fast-changing parts talk over APIs, so there is no single chokepoint to watch.

options.text: Service-to-service traffic is encrypted with mTLS, which hides payloads from sensors
options.why: True, mTLS limits what network sensors can inspect, but it isn't the core reason. Even unencrypted, there's no single perimeter to watch across many short-lived components.

options.text: The provider manages the serverless runtime, so runtime threats are its responsibility
options.why: The first half is true: the provider manages the serverless runtime. But the customer still owns function code, permissions and configuration, and this doesn't explain why perimeter monitoring falls short.

options.text: Containers are replaced so often that logs are lost before they can be collected
options.why: True only when logs stay inside the container. Shipping them off centrally fixes that. It's a logging-design issue, not the reason perimeter monitoring falls short.

explanation: The core cloud-native challenge is the distributed, ephemeral attack surface. Monitoring has to follow the workloads and APIs, using cloud-native tools.

stem: A vendor advisory describes a flaw that lets code in a guest VM execute on the underlying host. What is this attack, and what is the primary mitigation?

options.text: VM escape; keep the hypervisor patched and apply the vendor's fix
options.why: Correct. Breaking out of the guest's isolation is VM escape, the most severe virtualisation-specific attack. Patching the hypervisor closes it.

options.text: VM sprawl; inventory every VM and reconcile it against the asset list
options.why: Sprawl is about forgotten, unmanaged VMs, not breaking isolation.

options.text: VM escape; snapshot every guest so it can be rolled back if hit
options.why: Right attack, wrong fix: snapshots help recovery but don't prevent the escape, and they can hold sensitive data themselves.

options.text: Container escape; stop running workloads as root on the host
options.why: Adjacent concept, wrong technology: the advisory describes a guest VM and a hypervisor, not containers.

explanation: VM escape bypasses isolation and can expose every VM on the host, which makes hypervisor patching critical.

stem: This reconciliation report was produced during a quarterly review. What issue does it show, and what is the BEST next step?
artifact:
VM inventory reconciliation (cluster: prod-esx-02)
VM name        Power  Guest OS             Last patched  In asset list?
fin-app-01     On     Windows Server 2022  2026-09-28    yes
test-sql-old   On     Windows Server 2016  2023-11-02    no
jdoe-poc-web   On     Ubuntu 20.04         2024-02-19    no
hr-portal-02   On     Ubuntu 24.04         2026-10-01    yes

options.text: VM sprawl: find owners for the unlisted VMs, then patch and register or decommission them
options.why: Correct. Running VMs missing from the asset list, unpatched for years, are textbook sprawl and easy targets.

options.text: VM escape risk: patch the prod-esx-02 hypervisors before anything else on the cluster
options.why: Wrong problem: nothing shows a guest breaking isolation. Patching hypervisors is good hygiene but leaves two unowned, unpatched VMs running.

options.text: VM sprawl: add the two VMs to the asset list now so the inventory matches the cluster
options.why: Scope: it fixes the paperwork, not the risk. The VMs stay unpatched with nobody responsible for them.

options.text: VM sprawl: run a credentialed vulnerability scan of the two unlisted VMs and file the report
options.why: Order: the scan will confirm what's already clear (years unpatched), but with no owner nobody acts on the report. Find the owner first.

explanation: Inventory VMs regularly and cross-reference them with the active asset list. Unknown VMs need an owner, then patching or decommissioning.

stem: An analyst suspects lateral movement between two VMs on the same host, but the perimeter firewall logs show nothing. What would BEST give visibility of this traffic?

options.text: Micro-segmentation and monitoring at the virtual network layer, e.g. VMware NSX
options.why: Correct. East-west traffic between VMs never crosses the perimeter, so visibility has to come from inside the virtual network.

options.text: Add deny-and-log rules for the two VMs' subnets on the perimeter firewall
options.why: Scope: traffic between VMs on one host never reaches the perimeter, so these rules never see it.

options.text: Enable NetFlow export on the core switch uplinks serving the hypervisor host
options.why: Scope: NetFlow at the core sees traffic leaving the host. VM-to-VM traffic on the same host stays on the virtual switch.

options.text: Review the hypervisor's snapshot-creation and VM-migration events for attacker activity
options.why: True, these events matter in investigations, but they don't show network traffic between VMs.

explanation: East-west traffic between VMs stays inside the host or virtual switch. Micro-segmentation tools give the virtual network layer both visibility and control.

stem: During a test, an attacker breaks out of a compromised container. Why can the impact be greater than a single compromised application?

options.text: The host kernel is shared, so an escape can reach the host and all its other containers
options.why: Correct. The shared kernel is the core container risk.

options.text: The image probably contains unpatched packages the attacker can exploit for access
options.why: True, unpatched images are a common entry point, but that's how the container was compromised, not why breaking out has a bigger blast radius.

options.text: Kubernetes reschedules the compromised container onto other nodes when it restarts
options.why: False as stated: Kubernetes restarts pods from the image, not the attacker's running state. The wider impact comes from the shared kernel.

options.text: The pod's service-account token gives the attacker cluster-admin rights over the cluster
options.why: Only if RBAC is misconfigured. Service-account tokens are limited by RBAC and don't grant cluster-admin by default. Escape impact comes from the shared kernel.

explanation: Containers are lightweight because they share the host kernel. That same sharing means a container escape can compromise the host and its neighbours.

stem: This Falco alert fires for a production pod. What is the BEST interpretation and response?
artifact:
10:42:17.311 Notice A shell was spawned in a container with an attached terminal
  rule=Terminal shell in container  user=root  shell=bash  parent=runc
  k8s.ns=prod  k8s.pod=payments-api-7d9f6c-x2kqp
  image=registry.example.com/payments-api:2.3.1

options.text: Interactive root shell in prod: check the k8s audit log for who ran exec, then contain the pod
options.why: Correct. Interactive shells in production containers are rare and risky. The audit log shows the API-level who and how.

options.text: Delete the pod right away so the Deployment replaces it with a clean replica
options.why: Order: it contains the threat but destroys the evidence (processes, files, memory) before you know who got in or how.

options.text: Rescan the payments-api:2.3.1 image with Trivy and close the alert if it comes back clean
options.why: Wrong phase: an image scan is a pre-deployment control. It says nothing about who is running commands in the live container.

options.text: Block registry.example.com at egress so no further compromised images can be pulled
options.why: Scope: nothing shows the image is compromised, and the shell is already running. Blocking the registry doesn't touch the live session.

explanation: Falco gives runtime visibility inside containers, and the Kubernetes audit log gives API-level visibility (e.g. who ran kubectl exec). Together they are the analyst's main tools.

stem: A security review of the company's Kubernetes clusters is being scoped. Which TWO findings are common Kubernetes-specific attack vectors? (Choose two.)

options.text: Overly permissive RBAC role bindings granting broad cluster rights
options.why: Correct. RBAC misconfiguration is a top Kubernetes attack vector.

options.text: Secrets stored in plaintext in manifests or environment variables
options.why: Correct. Plaintext secrets are easy to steal once an attacker has any foothold.

options.text: Separate namespaces for each team's workloads within the same cluster
options.why: Adjacent concept: namespaces are an isolation control, not an attack vector (though they don't enforce security boundaries by themselves).

options.text: Falco deployed as a DaemonSet so every node is monitored at runtime
options.why: Adjacent concept: this is a detection control, not an attack vector.

explanation: Top Kubernetes attack vectors: RBAC misconfigurations, exposed API servers and plaintext secrets.

stem: Developers want to deploy a popular image straight from a public registry to production. Which control should be applied FIRST?

options.text: Scan it for vulnerabilities (e.g. Trivy) and promote it through a trusted internal registry
options.why: Correct. Scanning before deployment is the core image-security control.

options.text: Sign the image with the team's key and push it to the internal registry for deployment
options.why: Scope: signing proves where an image came from once you've accepted it. It doesn't find vulnerabilities or malware already inside it.

options.text: Deploy it to staging and watch Falco runtime alerts for a week before promoting it
options.why: Timing: Falco is runtime detection. Known-vulnerable packages should be caught by a scan before anything runs.

options.text: Pin the image to a specific digest so the same version is deployed every time
options.why: Reproducibility, not security: pinning a vulnerable image just deploys the same vulnerabilities consistently.

explanation: Never pull public images blindly. Scan them before deployment (Trivy, Prisma Cloud) and apply least privilege at the container level.

stem: An analyst reviews these API gateway logs. What BEST describes the activity?
artifact:
gw-access.log (api.example.com)
2026-10-09T14:03:11Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10231 200 1.2KB
2026-10-09T14:03:11Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10232 200 1.1KB
2026-10-09T14:03:12Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10233 200 1.3KB
2026-10-09T14:03:12Z 198.51.100.77 user=cust_4410 GET /api/v1/invoices/10234 200 1.2KB
... 1,812 similar requests in 6 minutes, all HTTP 200

options.text: BOLA enumeration: one customer's token is retrieving other customers' invoices
options.why: Correct. Sequential object IDs, all returning 200 to a single user, mean the API isn't checking that the caller owns each object.

options.text: Credential stuffing: breached passwords replayed against the API's login endpoint
options.why: Scope: the requests are already authenticated and target invoice objects, not the login endpoint.

options.text: An unauthenticated scraper brute-forcing invoice IDs on a public endpoint
options.why: Scope: every request is authenticated as cust_4410. The flaw is that the API doesn't check who owns each object.

options.text: Normal pagination by a client app syncing the customer's invoice history
options.why: Pagination uses page or offset parameters over one customer's data. Walking sequential object IDs across customers isn't normal.

explanation: BOLA, top of the OWASP API Security Top 10, lets an authenticated user access objects they don't own by changing IDs. API gateways should alert on sequential enumeration patterns.

stem: The billing-sync service's API key normally calls the API from 192.0.2.15. The gateway now shows the activity below. What should the analyst do FIRST?
artifact:
api-key: key_live_8f3a...c21 (owner: billing-sync service)
2026-10-09T01:12:44Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?limit=500 200
2026-10-09T01:12:51Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?offset=500&limit=500 200
2026-10-09T01:13:02Z src=203.0.113.200 GET /api/v1/customers?offset=1000&limit=500 200

options.text: Revoke and rotate the key, then find how it leaked and what data it reached
options.why: Correct. A key used from an unexpected location while bulk-pulling customer data means stopping the exfiltration is the priority.

options.text: Add a rate limit to the customers endpoint to slow the bulk download
options.why: Scope: this slows the theft but doesn't stop it. The key is still valid.

options.text: Block 203.0.113.200 at the API gateway and keep the key active for billing-sync
options.why: Scope: the attacker can switch IP addresses. The stolen key keeps working from anywhere else.

options.text: Export the key's full request history to scope the exposure before changing anything
options.why: Order: scoping matters, but customer records are leaving right now. Contain first, then scope.

explanation: API keys and OAuth tokens are the primary API credentials, and key leakage is a major attack vector. Monitor for keys used from unexpected locations. When it happens, revoke first, then scope and find the leak (e.g. a committed secret).

stem: A company exposes dozens of REST APIs to partners. Where is the BEST place to centrally log and control API activity, such as authentication failures and request rates?

options.text: The API gateway in front of the services
options.why: Correct. It sits in front of the APIs and can authenticate, rate-limit and log every call.

options.text: The perimeter next-generation firewall
options.why: It inspects sessions at the edge, but it can't authenticate, rate-limit or log per API key, user and object the way a gateway does.

options.text: EDR agents on the servers hosting the APIs
options.why: Scope: EDR sees processes on the hosts, not API-level details, and it can't apply controls like rate limiting.

options.text: The SIEM, via forwarded web-server access logs
options.why: True, a SIEM can correlate API logs, but it only observes. It can't authenticate, rate-limit or block calls.

explanation: API gateways are the main point for monitoring and controlling API activity. Log everything there and watch for auth failures, high request rates and enumeration.

stem: Why do API attacks often get past traditional network security tools?

options.text: REST calls travel over HTTP(S) and look the same as ordinary web traffic
options.why: Correct. Without API-aware inspection, an attack request looks the same as a legitimate one.

options.text: APIs usually listen on non-standard ports that firewalls don't watch
options.why: False: most REST APIs use standard HTTPS on port 443, which is exactly why they blend in.

options.text: APIs exchange binary formats like gRPC that IDS signatures can't decode
options.why: Partly true for gRPC, but most APIs are REST with JSON over HTTPS. Their attacks are missed because they look like normal web traffic.

options.text: Authenticated API calls are treated as trusted by network security tools
options.why: A misconception: network tools don't see or trust API authentication. The problem is that malicious calls look like legitimate web requests.

explanation: API attacks blend into normal web traffic, which is why API-aware monitoring at the gateway matters.

stem: Contractors will use their personal phones for corporate email and files. Legal says the company must not control or wipe the whole device. Which approach fits BEST?

options.text: Mobile Application Management (MAM) for corporate apps and data only
options.why: Correct. MAM manages only corporate apps and data, the right fit for BYOD.

options.text: Mobile Device Management (MDM) enrolment of each contractor's phone
options.why: MDM manages the entire device, which goes beyond what Legal allows here.

options.text: An EDR-style mobile threat defence app installed on each phone
options.why: Scope: it detects threats on the device but doesn't separate or control the corporate data.

options.text: Require full-device encryption and a PIN before email access
options.why: Scope: this protects data at rest if the phone is lost, but can't control or remove corporate data in apps.

explanation: MDM manages corporate-owned devices end to end. MAM manages corporate apps and data only, which makes it the BYOD choice.

stem: An analyst reviews this conditional access sign-in log. Which entry should be investigated FIRST?
artifact:
Conditional access sign-ins
Time   User      Device        Compliant  Policy result  Outcome
07:58  a.lim     LT-0412       Yes        Grant (MFA)    Success
08:03  r.osman   LT-0377       No         Block          Failure
08:11  k.wong    unregistered  No         Not applied    Success
08:15  a.lim     LT-0412       Yes        Grant (MFA)    Success

options.text: 08:11 k.wong: success from an unregistered, non-compliant device, policy not applied
options.why: Correct. An unexpected success is a gap in zero-trust enforcement, a possible bypass or misconfiguration.

options.text: 08:03 r.osman: blocked sign-in from the non-compliant laptop LT-0377
options.why: The policy worked as intended. Follow up on the device's compliance later; it isn't the urgent item.

options.text: 07:58 a.lim: first sign-in of the day from LT-0412 with MFA satisfied
options.why: A normal, expected sign-in: compliant device, MFA satisfied.

options.text: 08:15 a.lim: second sign-in from LT-0412 within 20 minutes of the first
options.why: Repeated compliant, MFA-backed sign-ins from the same device are normal.

explanation: Monitor conditional access logs for compliance failures and, more importantly, unexpected successes. Access that should have been checked but wasn't is the real risk.

stem: Facilities wants to connect smart HVAC sensors and lobby displays to the office network. These devices can't run EDR or be enrolled in management. What is the BEST control?

options.text: Put them on a dedicated, segmented VLAN with tightly restricted access
options.why: Correct. If you can't manage a device, contain it. Segmentation limits what a compromised IoT device can reach.

options.text: Place them in the DMZ alongside the internet-facing web servers
options.why: Wrong segment: the DMZ is for internet-facing services. IoT devices there are more exposed and sit next to servers you care about.

options.text: Enrol them in the UEM console so their compliance can be tracked
options.why: The stem says they can't be enrolled. UEM needs a supported OS or agent, so it can't manage these devices.

options.text: Keep them on the corporate VLAN but add them to the weekly vulnerability scans
options.why: Scope: scanning finds weaknesses but doesn't limit what a compromised device can reach.

explanation: IoT devices are high risk and usually can't be managed with standard tools. Segment them away from corporate systems.

stem: During an investigation, an analyst must quickly list which company devices accessed a file server last week and whether each was patched and compliant. What is the BEST starting point?

options.text: The UEM console covering the whole device fleet
options.why: Correct. UEM manages the whole device fleet from one console, the starting point for inventory and compliance checks.

options.text: The perimeter firewall's connection logs
options.why: These show connections at the edge, not device inventory or compliance state.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the internal device range
options.why: Timing and scope: a new scan shows today's vulnerabilities, not last week's access or each device's compliance.

options.text: The file server's SMB access logs for last week
options.why: True, these show which devices connected, but not whether each was patched and compliant.

explanation: UEM is the modern single console for the full fleet: inventory, compliance and posture during investigations.
